edges.qualification: Land and water legs can form one delivery chain; not all trips use both.

scope.configuration: Roman multimodal freight chains represented in the cost discussions.

alternatives: Water-only trips where both endpoints are directly accessible
edges.dispute: Mode shares and actual trip chains are not observed by ORBIS.

edges.qualification: For accessible origin/destination pairs, alternative routes may trade off line-haul and transfer costs.

scope.configuration: Lowland British pottery distribution c. 250–400 CE.

edges.dispute: Relative costs are inferred from pottery; other cargoes may rank modes differently.

edges.qualification: Additional handling and access costs can reduce the apparent advantage inferred from water line-haul rates alone.

scope.configuration: End-to-end chain with transfers, storage and port access.

alternatives: Long direct bulk voyages with few transfers
edges.dispute: Actual components are not independently priced for every ancient route.

edges.qualification: Model seasonality changes feasible/time-cost routes without implying universal winter closure.

scope.configuration: ORBIS v1 seasonal sailing scenarios.

edges.dispute: Weather simulations use proxy/model inputs; actual traveler risk tolerances are unobserved.

edges.qualification: Wayside provisions and engineering support an integrated road system.

scope.configuration: Inka network integration described by ICOMOS, with local variation.

alternatives: Use pre-existing paths and local hospitality
edges.dispute: Presence of facilities does not establish uniform service levels or voluntary access.

edges.qualification: Scarcity shapes the inferred mode and intensity of traffic on a specific desert segment.

scope.configuration: Cachiyuyo de Llampos desert road, not all Andean roads.

edges.dispute: Traffic composition is inferred; occasional pack-animal transport remains possible.

edges.qualification: Road traffic and logistics plausibly broaden local craft exchange.

scope.configuration: Non-Inka mining/craft camps and roadside sites in Garrido’s survey area.

edges.dispute: Indirect imperial control or taxation can coexist with household-looking material remains.

edges.qualification: Guarantees allocated financial risk and supported early private concessions.

scope.configuration: Guaranteed British-owned Indian railway companies from the 1850s.

edges.dispute: Counterfactual necessity of guarantees is contested; payments do not establish excessive investor returns.

edges.qualification: State priorities selected and authorized routes, including strategic links.

scope.configuration: Government of India line placement; motives differed by line.

edges.dispute: Military, commercial and humanitarian objectives interacted; their weights are not separately estimated.

edges.qualification: Reduced transport costs and larger trading opportunities are supported by the district/commodity evidence.

scope.configuration: Donaldson’s colonial district and trade panel.

edges.dispute: Nonrandom placement and model assumptions remain; no universal household welfare claim.

edges.qualification: Employment reductions accompany state purchases and expense savings in the company panel.

scope.configuration: Colonial takeover under preset contract dates and treasury incentives.

edges.dispute: Direct wages and workers’ later occupations are missing; all service quality is not observed.

edges.qualification: Rail access supports cocoa cultivation/shipment in the studied areas.

scope.configuration: Ghana forest-zone railway access, 1901–1931.

edges.dispute: Selection toward cocoa potential and movement of production complicate causal interpretation.

edges.qualification: Earlier access is linked to the emergence of trading towns.

scope.configuration: Ghana rail proximity and settlement growth, 1901–1931.

edges.dispute: Does not prove national welfare gains or that every nearby place benefited.

edges.qualification: Service and repair financing contributed to sustaining operation; deterioration participated in a revenue/maintenance feedback.

scope.configuration: Ghana railway decline after 1974.

edges.dispute: Historical narrative does not separately identify finance, management and demand shocks.

edges.qualification: Road services expanded while rail traffic and cocoa share declined.

scope.configuration: Ghana post-independence transport through 2000; incomplete rather than total rail elimination.

edges.dispute: Roads partly followed existing rail places; displacement is not a clean randomized treatment.

edges.qualification: Established towns may coordinate later investment even after loss of relative rail access.

scope.configuration: Ghana’s census/spatial outcomes through 2000.

edges.dispute: Coordination is harder to identify uniquely than the observed persistence itself.

edges.qualification: Managed service retained technical responsibility rather than requiring every passenger to maintain a vehicle.

scope.configuration: EVC electric-cab service, starting New York 1897.

edges.dispute: Operational specialization did not establish profitability or successful scaling.

edges.qualification: Battery limitations were among operational constraints; they are not assigned all explanatory weight for EVC failure.

scope.configuration: Early electric-cab service and initial-generation battery operation.

edges.dispute: Business/finance shocks and technical shortcomings are not causally decomposed.

edges.qualification: Disciplined fleet maintenance supports defined later electric tasks.

scope.configuration: Electric commercial/specialized fleet use in the comparative early-twentieth-century record.

edges.dispute: Conditional fleet viability does not demonstrate general private-car parity.

edges.qualification: Documented association activity attempted to improve charging access, utility use and compatibility; an incremental uptake effect is not established.

scope.configuration: US utility-supported EV applications after EVAA formation in 1909.

edges.dispute: This edge represents the proposed complementary mechanism, not a measured adoption effect; some activities were promotional or prospective.

edges.qualification: Gasoline’s general private-car position expanded while electric passenger-car production contracted.

scope.configuration: US private-car market in the 1910s–1920s; specialty fleet tasks excluded.

edges.dispute: No precise modal share or single-cause explanation; price, range, maintenance and use culture interacted.

edges.qualification: Compatible dimensions and handling specifications eased investment across firms/modes.

scope.configuration: Postwar US/ISO standardized container systems.

edges.dispute: This is not a claim that the exact adopted standards were technically necessary or socially optimal.

edges.qualification: Cranes and inland/port facilities made intermodal handling practical at scale.

scope.configuration: 1950s–1980s port/rail/truck container systems.

edges.dispute: Multiple complementary inputs are observed; this edge alone asserts no joint sufficiency or universal necessary bundle.

edges.qualification: Vietnam logistics demand supported capacity and use in the historical account.

scope.configuration: US military container shipments after 1965 and related capacity.

edges.dispute: No isolated military-demand treatment effect; not necessary for every route or country.

edges.qualification: Bargaining changed work rules and financed adjustment during West Coast mechanization; it did not alone cause container uptake.

scope.configuration: 1960 agreement and 1961–1966 fund; not all countries’ labour institutions.

edges.dispute: Agreement covered mechanization more broadly than containers and did not eliminate later conflicts.

edges.qualification: Container handling removed/reduced repeated unpacked dock tasks in the court’s historical account.

scope.configuration: US West Coast dock tasks in the 1960s–1970s.

edges.dispute: Task loss does not equal one-for-one job loss, and aggregate employment not estimated.

edges.qualification: Intermodal containers allowed stuffing and unstuffing to take place away from docks.

scope.configuration: West Coast container freight stations and owner premises.

edges.dispute: New task locations created competing labour claims; worker welfare at each location is not measured.

edges.qualification: Official account attributes expansion to state planning and allocation of scarce waterfront space.

scope.configuration: Singapore terminals 1972–2000, especially Pasir Panjang.

alternatives: Other sites/staged expansion; costs not inspected
edges.dispute: Primary official rationale, not independent proof that the selected site or plan was uniquely optimal.

edges.qualification: The 2000 government account identifies workforce upgrading and information services as complements; their distinct contribution is not independently measured.

scope.configuration: Singapore’s Pasir Panjang terminal opening and prior upgrading.

alternatives: Alternative staffing/service organization; comparative evidence absent
edges.dispute: Training access and worker outcomes are not measured; official success language may omit losses.
